per_quote.text: The goal of the present research was to examine how political climate moderates the relationship between self-reported political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.
However, conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions.
We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023.
We assessed regional political climate using zip code data provided by participants and 2020 presidential election results sourced from the New York Times [22].

Political conservatism and conservative regional climate were both associated with higher levels of COVID-19 vaccine and booster hesitancy and lower rates of self-reported vaccination and boosting, when controlling for age, education, income, and race.
As political conservatism increases vaccine hesitancy also increases, but this increase is even greater for individuals who live in a more conservative regional climate.
The interaction for vaccination was not significant, this difference between attitudes (hesitancy) and action (vaccination), likely reflects the high prevalence of COVID-19 vaccine mandates.
liberals were less likely to be hesitant regardless of political climate.

By looking at political orientation and region climate, we identify a novel and important finding, specifically that conservative individuals are more likely to received booster doses in liberal regions.
Regional factors (e.g., population density) may play a role in linking 2020 election votes to vaccine attitudes and behaviors.
Self-report is susceptible to social desirability [30] and recall bias [31], and we cannot assume that reported vaccine status reflects actual vaccine status.
Further, our sample includes only White and Black participants recruited through Qualtrics Panels, and may not generalize to broader populations in the United States.
Finally, it should be noted that this data is cross-sectional and we cannot assume causal or directional associations.

While previous research has identified the unique impact of both political orientation and political climate on vaccination attitudes, there has been little research on the interaction between personal political orientation and local political climate.
Previous studies have focused on either political orientation or political climate.
This study introduces a novel computational approach to measure subnational and event-driven variation in partisan polarization and explores these dynamics across the United States and Canada.

Our analysis reveals that politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries, with this effect particularly pronounced in the United States.

this study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties.
Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship.
However, unlike what is often observed in studies of other adolescent populations, substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties.
Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation.
Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.
First, we recognize that the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time

By focusing on reservation schools, where AI youth are the norm rather than a statistical minority, this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research and contributes new insights into the unique architecture of AI adolescent social worlds.

Research in diverse school settings has consistently demonstrated that substance use is linked to friendship ties, often through processes of selection (youth choosing friends with similar behaviors) and influence (friends shaping one another’s conduct)
